Series::diag_embed¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::diag_embed() const -> Series
Series::diag_embed(std::int64_t diagonal) const -> Series
Series::diag_embed(std::int64_t diagonal, std::int64_t dim1, std::int64_t dim2) const -> Series

What It Does¶

diag_embed() turns the last axis of the input into a diagonal. Every leading axis is a batch axis, so a [batch, n] input becomes batch separate n x n diagonal matrices, and a plain vector becomes a single diagonal matrix.

For an input of shape [b0, b1, ..., n] the result holds, for every batch index, a square plane of side n + abs(diagonal) that is zero everywhere except along the requested diagonal. The plane’s two axes are placed at dim1 and dim2 of the result, which by default are the last two.

To build a single diagonal matrix from a multi-axis input by flattening it first, use diagflat().

Overload Map¶

diag_embed()

Main diagonal, plane in the last two axes.

diag_embed(std::int64_t diagonal)

Shifts the write target: positive values place the diagonal above the main diagonal, negative values below it.

diag_embed(std::int64_t diagonal, std::int64_t dim1, std::int64_t dim2)

Offset diagonal and explicit placement of the plane’s two axes in the result.

Parameters¶

diagonal (std::int64_t)

The diagonal offset. If the last axis has n values, each plane has side n + abs(diagonal).

dim1, dim2 (std::int64_t)

Where the plane’s row axis and column axis go in the result (which has one more axis than the input). Negative values count from the end of the result. They must refer to different axes. The default is (-2, -1). The offset is measured from dim1 toward dim2, so swapping them mirrors the plane.

Returns¶

Series Rank input.dim() + 1: the batch axes in order, with the two plane axes inserted at dim1 and dim2.

Gradient¶

diag_embed() is differentiable. The reverse pass reads each input value back from the diagonal position it was written to; every other position of the result contributes nothing.

Examples¶

Example 1. A 1D input becomes a square diagonal matrix.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({4, 5, 6}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64).diag_embed();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=9, contiguous=true)
data=[[4, 0, 0],
  [0, 5, 0],
  [0, 0, 6]]

Example 2. A positive offset moves the diagonal above the main diagonal and grows the matrix by abs(diagonal).

std::cout << pluss::make_series({4, 5, 6}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64).diag_embed(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[4,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=16, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 4, 0, 0],
  [0, 0, 5, 0],
  [0, 0, 0, 6],
  [0, 0, 0, 0]]

Example 3. Leading axes are batch axes: each row becomes its own matrix.

auto rows = pluss::make_series({
    {1, 2},
    {3, 4},
}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

std::cout << rows.diag_embed();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2,2], strides=[4,2,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=8, contiguous=true)
data=[[[1, 0],
  [0, 2]],
  [[3, 0],
  [0, 4]]]

The 2 x 2 input becomes a stack of two 2 x 2 diagonal matrices, shape [2, 2, 2], one per row.

Example 4. dim1 and dim2 choose where the plane’s axes land in the result.

auto rows = pluss::make_series({
    {1, 2, 3},
    {4, 5, 6},
}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

auto moved = rows.diag_embed(0, 0, 1);
std::cout << moved.sizes()[0] << " " << moved.sizes()[1] << " " << moved.sizes()[2] << "\n";
std::cout << moved;

Output¶

3 3 2
pluss::Series(shape=[3,3,2], strides=[3,1,9], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=18, contiguous=false)
data=[[[1, 4],
  [0, 0],
  [0, 0]],
  [[0, 0],
  [2, 5],
  [0, 0]],
  [[0, 0],
  [0, 0],
  [3, 6]]]

With the plane at axes (0, 1), the batch axis moves to the end: element moved[i, j, b] is the plane entry (i, j) of batch b.

Example 5. Reverse-mode reads sensitivity back from the embedded diagonal.

auto diag_embed_grad = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
diag_embed_grad.tracks_slope_(true);
diag_embed_grad.diag_embed().sum().reverse();

std::cout << diag_embed_grad.sensitivity();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1, 1]

Example 6. The two plane axes must differ.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64).diag_embed(0, 1, 1) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

diag_embed: dim1 and dim2 must differ

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The last axis is the one embedded; every other axis is preserved as a batch axis. This differs from diagflat(), which flattens the whole input first.

  • Offsets increase each plane’s side by abs(diagonal); all non-diagonal positions are zero.

  • dim1 and dim2 index the result, which has one more axis than the input.

  • A scalar (rank-0) input has no axis to embed and fails.

Summary¶

diag_embed() writes the last axis of the input onto a diagonal of new planes:

  • leading axes are batch axes and are preserved

  • diagonal shifts the diagonal and grows the plane

  • dim1/dim2 place the plane in the result

  • differentiable; diagflat() is the flatten-first alternative
